strengths: Novel and well-motivated reframing of multi-agent coordination as an in-context learning problem (Hidden-Utility Markov Game), extending Decision-Pretrained Transformer ideas to partner adaptation rather than task adaptation, which is a reasonably fresh angle relative to prior ICRL/opponent-modeling work.

Broad empirical evaluation across five Overcooked layouts with several relevant and reasonably strong baselines (BC, MEP, HSP, HSP fine-tuning, and a PEARL-inspired meta-RL baseline), rather than comparing against only weak baselines.

A genuine human-subject study (36 participants, consent obtained, blinded agent identities, quantitative rankings plus qualitative feedback) that goes beyond policy-vs-policy evaluation and lends some external validity to the claims.

Useful analyses of adaptation dynamics (speed of adaptation, robustness to non-stationary/partner-swapped scenarios) and ablations on context length and trajectory shuffling that shed light on design choices.
Strong reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, dataset generation procedure, hardware/timing information, and algorithm pseudocode provided in the appendix.
Honest limitations section and appropriate disclosure of LLM usage.
weaknesses: The main quantitative comparison in Table 1 partially conflates training conditions: MEP/HSP baselines are trained with dense reward shaping while COOT uses only sparse rewards, described by the authors themselves as giving baselines an 'upper-bound' advantage; this complicates a clean attribution of COOT's gains to the proposed in-context mechanism versus reward setup differences.

The claim that COOT 'consistently outperforms' baselines is somewhat overstated: in Coord. Ring, COOT's reward (38.3) is actually lower than HSP/HSP-ft (41.1/41.3) and within one std of several baselines, and in Asymm. Adv. HSP/HSP-ft edge out COOT; the paper's narrative downplays these near-ties.

The evaluation partners, while nominally 'unseen', are generated from the same event-based hidden-reward mechanism (and often the same policy pool machinery, e.g., ZSC-Eval checkpoints) used to construct the training distribution for COOT, raising the question of whether the demonstrated generalization is truly out-of-distribution or largely in-distribution generalization within a fairly narrow behavioral family.

Several key ablations and robustness analyses have limited statistical rigor: the non-stationary partner-swap experiment (Table 4) reports single adaptation-episode counts for only 6 partner-swap pairs with no variance estimates, and the context-length ablation (Table 9) reports single-run point rewards without confidence intervals, making it hard to assess significance of the reported trends.

The meta-RL baseline (HSP-meta/PEARL-style) underperforming even vanilla HSP is surprising and could reflect an under-tuned or poorly suited implementation (reconstruction loss, joint training instability) rather than a fundamental shortcoming of trajectory-conditioned meta-RL approaches in general, weakening the generality of the claim that meta-RL 'struggles' at this task.

Human study is restricted to a single layout (Coord. Ring) and 36 participants split across only 4 agents, which limits the extent to which the human-preference results can be generalized across the more coordination-heavy layouts (e.g., Multi-recipe) where the largest gaps against policy-based partners were observed.

No direct empirical comparison to closely related in-context/partner-modeling methods explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., PECAN, Algorithm Distillation-style opponent modeling), leaving open how COOT compares to the most directly relevant prior in-context coordination approaches beyond citation.

The model is a small GPT-2-style transformer evaluated only in the Overcooked domain family; there is no evidence of scalability to larger/more complex or continuous-action coordination settings, and no theoretical justification for why in-context best-response prediction should converge or generalize well beyond the empirical results shown.

strengths: The paper reframes in-context learning for multi-agent coordination as a partner-generalization problem (rather than task-generalization), which is a clear and well-motivated conceptual shift from prior ICRL/DPT work, formalized via the Hidden-Utility Markov Game.

Extensive empirical evaluation across two distinct benchmarks (Overcooked with 5 layouts, and GRF 3v1), with a broad set of baselines including population-based methods (HSP, MEP), gradient-based fine-tuning, meta-RL context methods (HSP-meta, PACE), and additional appendix baselines (GAMMA, PLASTIC).

A well-designed human study (IRB-approved, 36 participants, double-blind agent ordering) with both quantitative metrics (return, collaboration/adaptivity ratings, best-agent selection) and a qualitative analysis of open-ended feedback that corroborates the quantitative advantage of CooT.

Thorough ablation studies covering context length, data augmentation strategies (temporal shuffling), data scale/diversity robustness, and adaptation to non-stationary partner switches, providing good insight into design choices.

Reasonable effort toward reproducibility and fair baseline comparison, including systematic hyperparameter search for HSP-meta to rule out under-tuning, sparse-reward-only baselines to isolate the effect of dense reward shaping, and detailed hyperparameters/hardware/algorithm pseudocode in the appendix.
Honest and specific limitations section (no explicit communication modeling, cold-start protocol, scaling to larger teams) rather than generic boilerplate.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: architecturally CooT is a direct application of Decision-Pretrained Transformers (Lee et al. 2023) to a multi-agent setting, with the main change being the training target (best-response actions vs. task-optimal actions) and data generation procedure; there is limited architectural or algorithmic novelty beyond this reframing.

Behavior-preferring partners are generated via linear combinations of hand-designed event features, which is a fairly narrow and synthetic model of partner diversity; although the human study helps validate generalization to real humans, the primary quantitative results rely heavily on this constructed partner space, and evaluation partners are drawn from the same underlying reward-function family as training partners (mitigated but not fully resolved by the overlap analyses in Appendix B.7).

Several headline results show overlapping standard deviations with the strongest baseline (e.g., Coord. Ring: CooT 38.30±3.71 vs. HSP 41.10±10.03, explicitly noted as tied by the authors' own bolding convention), which weakens the claim of consistent superiority across all settings.

GRF evaluation is limited to only three baselines (BC, MEP, HSP), omitting the more relevant context-based comparisons (HSP-meta, PACE) that are central to the paper's narrative, and is restricted to a single 3-vs-1 scenario, leaving scalability to larger, more complex teams unaddressed (though acknowledged as a limitation).

The human study, while methodologically sound, is conducted on a single layout (Coord. Ring) with a single default context configuration, limiting evidence that the observed human preference generalizes across the more coordination-heavy layouts where CooT's advantage over baselines was largest in the simulated evaluation.

The context-length ablation reveals a non-trivial degradation beyond 5 episodes that is only partially mitigated by context masking, and the underlying mechanism (outdated information) is diagnosed but not resolved, leaving an important design limitation for longer-horizon or continually shifting partners.

strengths: The paper conducts an unusually extensive empirical evaluation for a coordination paper: five Overcooked layouts, a GRF 3v1 scenario, a 36-participant IRB-approved human study with both quantitative and LLM-assisted qualitative coding of feedback, and a large battery of ablations (context length, temporal shuffling, dataset/partner scale, sparse-vs-dense reward baselines, sensitivity to evaluation-partner selection).

The framing of coordination as in-context 'partner generalization' rather than 'task generalization' is a reasonable and clearly articulated conceptual reframing of DPT-style in-context RL, and the paper explicitly relates this design choice to compounding-error theory (via the DPT regret bound) to argue why cross-episode context conditioning should be more robust than BC/BC-RNN.

Reproducibility materials are thorough: full hyperparameter tables, dataset construction algorithms (Algorithm 1/2), hardware/compute accounting, and an inference-time comparison table, which would allow a careful reader to reimplement the pipeline.

The authors proactively added several strengthening baselines/analyses in the appendix (GAMMA, PLASTIC, a PACE-augmented HSP-meta, sparse-reward-only HSP/MEP variants, partner-overlap and evaluation-set sensitivity checks) that address obvious reviewer concerns about confounds such as dense reward shaping and training/evaluation partner overlap.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is architecturally identical to DPT (Lee et al., 2023) with the same GPT-2 backbone; the primary change is the training-data construction (best-response actions against hidden-utility partners) rather than a new model or learning mechanism. This is a modest algorithmic novelty dressed in a new application framing.

The method's data-generation pipeline requires, for every training partner, jointly training a best-response policy via MAPPO to serve as the supervised target -- i.e., an oracle best-responder must already be solved offline for each of the 36 partners. This is a strong and somewhat underdiscussed requirement that is arguably just as data/compute-hungry as building the population pools used by HSP/MEP, undermining the paper's framing of COOT as more 'efficient' than population-based methods.

Several 'consistent outperformance' claims in the abstract/intro are not well supported by Table 1: on Coord. Ring and Asymm. Adv., HSP/HSP-ft are bolded as statistically tied or better, and many baselines have overlapping standard deviations with COOT (e.g., PACE at 4.43±9.02 has std larger than its mean). No significance tests (e.g., paired t-tests) are reported anywhere, despite fairly high variance across seeds, making it hard to assess whether the differences are reliable rather than noise.

The evaluation partner population is drawn from the same event-based hidden-utility reward space used to generate training partners (same HSP framework), so the 'diversity' checks (BR-div, JS-divergence) demonstrate behavioral dissimilarity within one synthetic reward family rather than true distributional shift; the only genuinely out-of-distribution test is the human study, which is confined to a single Overcooked layout (Coord. Ring), limiting the generality of the 'reliable for real-world human-AI collaboration' claim made in the abstract.

The human-study sample (36 participants, single layout, one round of 8 episodes per agent) is small relative to the strength of the claims drawn from it (e.g., 'preferred collaborator'), and the qualitative coding of open-ended comments relies on an LLM (Gemini 2.5 Flash) with only manual spot-checking rather than independent double-coding with inter-rater reliability, which weakens confidence in the adaptivity/negative-behavior counts reported in Table 21.

GRF evaluation is limited to a single 3v1 scenario and compares against only three baselines (BC, MEP, HSP), omitting the context-based competitors (PACE, HSP-meta) that are central comparisons in the Overcooked experiments, so the claim that COOT 'scales' to higher-dimensional/larger-team settings is only weakly substantiated.

The context-length ablation (best at 5 episodes, degrading beyond) is presented but not mechanistically explained beyond a post-hoc 'outdated information' hypothesis; no principled recency-weighting or attention analysis is provided, leaving this design choice largely empirical/ad hoc.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated reframing of in-context learning for multi-agent coordination: shifting the ICL objective from task generalization (as in DPT) to partner generalization, which is a sensible and underexplored angle on ad-hoc teamwork.

Extensive empirical evaluation across five Overcooked layouts and a GRF 3v1 scenario, compared against a broad and relevant set of baselines (BC/BC-RNN, HSP, MEP, HSP-ft, HSP-meta, PACE, plus GAMMA and PLASTIC in the appendix), with consistent gains in coordination-heavy layouts.

A well-designed and IRB-approved human study (36 participants) with both quantitative preference/return metrics and qualitative coding of open-ended feedback, providing convincing evidence that COOT's adaptive behavior is perceptible and preferred by real users, not just an artifact of policy-based evaluation.

Thorough ablation studies (context length, temporal shuffling strategies, dataset/partner scale) and robustness analyses (evaluation-partner sensitivity, population overlap checks) that substantially strengthen confidence in the reported effects.
Strong attention to reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, hardware/compute accounting, dataset construction procedures, and pseudocode for both training and evaluation pipelines.
Honest and specific limitations discussion (no communication modeling, cold-start protocol, restriction to non-embodied benchmarks) rather than generic boilerplate.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: the backbone and in-context learning objective are directly inherited from DPT (Lee et al., 2023), and the main innovation is the data-generation scheme (best-response conditioning under HU-MG), which itself borrows heavily from HSP's event-based reward construction. The paper's novelty is more conceptual/framing than architectural.

The GRF evaluation is narrow in scope (single 3v1 scenario, only 3 baselines: BC, MEP, HSP), which weakens the claim that COOT generalizes well to larger, higher-dimensional teams; the authors acknowledge scaling to larger teams remains future work, but the current evidence for 'scalability' is limited.

COOT relies on the same population of behavior-preferring/best-response agent pairs used by HSP/MEP for training, so part of its advantage may stem from the paradigm of conditioning on full interaction histories versus the specific pool—though the authors note this is a conservative comparison, disentangling 'paradigm advantage' from 'data advantage' is not fully rigorous.

Some ablation explanations (e.g., why context beyond 5 episodes degrades performance, why step-wise vs. chunk-wise shuffling differ) are described mainly as post-hoc hypotheses without deeper mechanistic analysis or additional interventions to confirm the proposed causes.

The human study is restricted to a single Overcooked layout (Coord. Ring) with a relatively small and demographically skewed participant pool (27 male vs 9 female), limiting how broadly the human-preference results can be generalized.

Several baseline results show very high variance (e.g., PACE's near-zero-mean results with large std in some layouts), and the paper's convention of bolding results 'within the best method's standard deviation' could visually inflate the apparent competitiveness of weaker/unstable baselines or obscure clear separations.

The theoretical justification in Appendix G linking COOT's few-shot convergence to DPT's regret bound is invoked somewhat loosely to argue against compounding errors, without direct empirical measurement of within-episode error accumulation to substantiate the claim.
